source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use the visual cue to help staff recognize fall risk while still using formal assessment and an individualized prevention plan.","B":"Treat the visual cue as a replacement for fall-risk assessment because the symbol alone determines which prevention measures are needed.","C":"Interpret the visual cue as a dietary marker because fall risk should not be communicated with bedside reminders for staff.","D":"Use the visual cue mainly to restrict visitors because limiting family contact is a standard intervention for preventing inpatient falls."}}
source_row.rationale: AHRQ Fall TIPS uses bedside tools to communicate patient-specific fall risks and prevention interventions while retaining formal risk assessment and individualized planning. Option A is correct. Option B incorrectly replaces assessment with the cue. Option C misclassifies the cue as dietary information. Option D incorrectly links fall-risk identification to visitor restriction.
source_row.source_detail: AHRQ — Fall TIPS: Patient-Centered Fall Prevention Toolkit: use formal fall-risk assessment, create an individualized prevention plan, and consistently execute it; bedside visual tools communicate patient-specific risks and interventions and do not replace assessment/planning. Current AHRQ Fall TIPS hospital toolkit; live federal resource rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: patient identification, specimen collection, asepsis, high-alert medication safeguards, fall prevention and communication that prevents safety events as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A hospital uses a bedside visual cue for clients assessed as high fall risk. What is the most appropriate interpretation of this practice?
